questions.prompt: How does Creon’s refusal to promise immediate exile differ from Oedipus’s earlier certainty in commanding others?
facilitatorNotes: He distinguishes his authority from the god’s and admits that he cannot see clearly enough to swear. This can be read as caution learned from the crisis, even though he still exercises firm power over the household.
evidence: I see no light; and, seeing not, I may not swear.

questions.prompt: How does Oedipus’s concern for his daughters extend the consequences beyond his own suffering?
facilitatorNotes: He anticipates social exclusion and damaged prospects for children who did not choose the events. His appeal asks Creon to offer care rather than transfer the father’s alleged guilt to them.
evidence: Neither think of them such sin

questions.prompt: What does the final warning ask an audience to reconsider about the opening image of the successful king?
facilitatorNotes: Past achievement and present prosperity cannot guarantee a life’s outcome. The Chorus’s retrospective scale challenges premature judgments of happiness without requiring readers to call the earlier saving of Thebes worthless.
evidence: Ere the full tale be finished

days.title: Hamlet — the witnesses on watch (I.1)
days.challenge: Distinguish directly observed appearance from the political and supernatural explanations attached to it.
days.focus: How dramatic interruptions test the authority of eyewitnesses.
days.context: This selection begins the play. Bernardo (Ber.) and Marcellus (Mar.) have seen an apparition; Horatio (Hor.), a scholar and friend of Prince Hamlet, initially doubts them. The dead King Hamlet and his living son have the same name. Stage directions belong to the edited play.
days.contentNote: The scene includes war, death, and Christian beliefs about ghosts. The printed dotted gap in Horatio’s speech is retained from this edition.

excerpt.locator: Hamlet, Act/scene I.I, source blocks 1–67; opens “Scene I. Elsinore. A platform before the castle.”; closes “Mar. Let's do't, I pray; and I this morning know Where we shall find him most conveniently. [Exeunt.”.

questions.prompt: What changes Horatio’s mind, and what remains unproved when he changes it?
facilitatorNotes: The appearance interrupts Bernardo’s attempted report and Horatio sees a figure resembling the dead king. His sensory evidence establishes an apparition within the drama, but does not establish its identity, purpose or moral trustworthiness. His own hesitation about its meaning matters.
evidence: Without the sensible and true avouch

questions.prompt: How does the military history make the ghost seem politically significant? Where does Horatio qualify that history?
facilitatorNotes: The armour recalls the dead king’s war with Norway, while preparations suggest his son’s generation will inherit the conflict. Horatio introduces the explanation as a whisper and an inference; likeness plus anxious circumstances can encourage a political reading without the silent ghost confirming it.
evidence: At least the whisper goes so.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of repeatedly commanding the ghost to speak and receiving no answer?
facilitatorNotes: The scholar’s learning and the soldiers’ force both fail to produce testimony. The audience shares the witnesses’ uncertainty, while the proposed meeting with Hamlet promises a new test. Alternatives can stress fear, suspense or limits of authority, provided they explain the silence.
evidence: Stay! speak, speak! I charge thee, speak!

days.title: Hamlet — public mourning and private grief (I.2)
days.challenge: Track changes between ceremonial speech, aside, solitary speech and questioning.
days.focus: Whether polished public language clarifies or controls private experience.
days.context: Claudius, the new king, has married Gertrude, his dead brother’s widow. Her son Hamlet remains in mourning. The scene moves from court ceremony to Hamlet alone, then to the watchers’ report.
days.contentNote: Hamlet expresses a wish for death and refers to suicide, without acting on it here. His misogynistic generalization is a character’s grieving judgment, not an established truth.

excerpt.locator: Hamlet, Act/scene I.II, source blocks 1–83; opens “Scene II. A room of state in the castle.”; closes “sit still, my soul: foul deeds will rise, Though all the earth o'erwhelm them, to men's eyes. [Exit.”.

questions.prompt: How do Claudius’s paired opposites present his marriage as reasonable?
facilitatorNotes: Funeral and marriage, joy and sorrow are placed in a balanced scale. The syntax presents incompatible feelings as measured statesmanship and claims the court’s assent. A reader may acknowledge real political needs while questioning how the performance suppresses objection.
evidence: In equal scale weighing delight and dole

questions.prompt: Why does Hamlet object to “seems” before later giving a speech nobody else hears?
facilitatorNotes: He distinguishes outward signs that can be performed from inward grief that exceeds them. The soliloquy then exposes the anger and despair hidden by his brief obedient public reply. His claim to inward truth need not make every generalization about his mother or women reliable.
evidence: But I have that within which passes show

questions.prompt: Compare Hamlet’s detailed questions about the apparition with his final suspicion of foul play. How far has the evidence taken him?
facilitatorNotes: Questions about armour, face, colour, duration and beard show an effort to test the account. The witnesses support a likeness and repeated appearance. Foul play is still a suspicion; no witness has heard the ghost allege murder. The movement from testing details to anticipating concealed crime should remain visible.
evidence: I doubt some foul play

days.title: Hamlet — advice and unequal freedom (I.3)
days.challenge: Read familiar maxims inside the unequal relationships that deliver them.
days.focus: How protective counsel, social status and control overlap.
days.context: Laertes prepares to return to France. He and his father Polonius advise Ophelia about Hamlet. Compare the permissions each young person receives instead of treating the speeches as an isolated collection of wise sayings.
days.contentNote: The dialogue assumes unequal sexual and social freedoms for women and men. Examine those assumptions through the characters’ actual words.

excerpt.locator: Hamlet, Act/scene I.III, source blocks 1–29; opens “Scene III. A room in Polonius's house.”; closes “Oph. I shall obey, my lord. [Exeunt.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Laertes say Hamlet’s will is not his own? Does that argument simply accuse Hamlet of lying?
facilitatorNotes: A prince’s marriage affects the state, so personal affection may not translate into an authorized commitment. Laertes explicitly allows that Hamlet may love her now; his warning concerns political constraint as well as youth and desire.
evidence: His greatness weigh'd, his will is not his own

questions.prompt: How does Ophelia answer her brother’s moral instruction without directly refusing it?
facilitatorNotes: She promises to guard her heart but warns him against preaching restraint while taking the easy path himself. The pastor comparison exposes a possible double standard and gives her a sharper critical voice than the final obedience alone would suggest.
evidence: the primrose path of dalliance

questions.prompt: Test “to thine own self be true” against Polonius’s instructions to Ophelia. What tension appears?
facilitatorNotes: The son receives advice about judgment, friendship and reputation while the daughter is told what to think and forbidden to talk to Hamlet. The maxim can mean integrity, prudent self-interest or consistency; the unequal freedom complicates an uncomplicated celebration of personal authenticity.
evidence: And with a larger tether may he walk

days.title: Hamlet — a command from the ghost (I.4–5)
days.challenge: Evaluate a powerful testimony while tracking emotional pressure and uncertain authority.
days.focus: The conversion of memory and filial love into a duty of revenge.
days.context: Hamlet joins Horatio and Marcellus on the watch. The apparition beckons him away. These two complete scenes continue directly from the previous night; the ghost’s account is testimony within the play, whose authority Hamlet must still consider.
days.contentNote: The ghost describes poisoning and bodily decay and urges revenge. Religious language reflects conflicting early modern beliefs about spirits, judgment and purification.

excerpt.locator: Hamlet, Act/scene I.IV, source blocks 1–36; Act/scene I.V, source blocks 1–65; opens “Scene IV. The platform.”; closes “ joint: O cursed spite, That ever I was born to set it right! Nay, come, let's go together. [Exeunt.”.

questions.prompt: How do Horatio and Hamlet assess the danger of following the ghost differently?
facilitatorNotes: Horatio imagines deception, a fatal location and a loss of reason; Hamlet minimizes his life’s value and treats an immortal soul as secure. Hamlet has named both heavenly and infernal possibilities, so following does not mean he has eliminated uncertainty.
evidence: What if it tempt you toward the flood

questions.prompt: What restrictions accompany the revenge command, and why might they be difficult to obey together?
facilitatorNotes: The ghost demands revenge while ordering Hamlet not to taint his mind or contrive against his mother. Its emotionally vivid accusation may intensify precisely the mental disturbance it forbids. Readers may differ about the command’s justice while identifying the conflict it creates.
evidence: Taint not thy mind

questions.prompt: How does Hamlet’s image of erasing his memory complicate the demand to remember?
facilitatorNotes: He imagines deleting learning, observation and earlier experience so that a single command fills his mind. Remembering the father becomes an act of narrowing the self, not simply preserving one additional fact. The closing complaint about setting time right reveals the burden beneath the oath.
evidence: I'll wipe away all trivial fond records

days.title: Hamlet — manufacturing an explanation (II.1)
days.challenge: Test whether a character’s method of gathering evidence can produce the answer he expects.
days.focus: Surveillance, planted allegations and a premature account of Hamlet’s distress.
days.context: Polonius sends his servant Reynaldo to inquire about Laertes in Paris. Ophelia then reports Hamlet’s alarming visit. Hamlet has told his friends that he may put on an “antic disposition”; Ophelia has not heard that plan.
days.contentNote: This scene includes surveillance, sexual allegations and a report of frightening physical contact. Its labels for mental distress belong to the characters.

excerpt.locator: Hamlet, Act/scene II.I, source blocks 1–41; opens “Scene I. A room in Polonius's house.”; closes “nown; which, being kept close, might move More grief to hide than hate to utter love. Come. [Exeunt.”.

questions.prompt: Why is Reynaldo instructed to tell lies, and what could make the resulting evidence unreliable?
facilitatorNotes: Polonius expects mild invented faults to tempt acquaintances into confirming more. The bait may also encourage agreement, gossip or elaboration, so a response can reflect the planted claim rather than independent knowledge. Reynaldo’s objection shows that the reputational cost is not invisible.
evidence: Your bait of falsehood takes this carp of truth

questions.prompt: What does Ophelia report directly, and what explanation does Polonius supply?
facilitatorNotes: She describes disordered clothing, physical trembling, staring, a sigh and his departure; she says she does not know the cause. Polonius immediately labels it love madness. Her observation may be careful even though the father’s causal explanation is premature.
evidence: Mad for thy love?

questions.prompt: Does Polonius’s admission of earlier error make his new conclusion secure?
facilitatorNotes: He admits he misread Hamlet’s courtship and that age can overreach in opinion. Yet he moves just as quickly to certainty that rejected access caused madness. Self-criticism and confidence coexist; the scene asks readers to examine the method, not simply choose one of his two judgments.
evidence: That hath made him mad.

days.title: Hamlet — the player’s tears and a proposed test (II.2 excerpt)
days.challenge: Follow an argument that changes direction inside an emotionally volatile soliloquy.
days.focus: The relation between imagined suffering, genuine feeling and evidence of guilt.
days.context: In omitted earlier parts of this scene, Claudius and Polonius discuss watching Hamlet; Rosencrantz and Guildenstern admit the court sent for them. A troupe now arrives. Hamlet requests a speech about the killing of the Trojan king Priam and the grief of his wife Hecuba. The first unlabelled welcome is Hamlet’s continuing speech.
days.contentNote: The recited tragedy includes violent killing. Hamlet uses abusive sexual language in his self-reproach; the discussion examines its rhetorical effect.

excerpt.locator: Hamlet, Act/scene II.II, source blocks 157–182; opens “Enter four or five Players.”; closes “ More relative than this. The play's the thing Wherein I'll catch the conscience of the king. [Exit.”.

questions.prompt: Why is Pyrrhus’s pause before killing Priam significant for a listener already troubled by delayed revenge?
facilitatorNotes: The recitation holds a violent avenger motionless before renewed action. It can mirror Hamlet’s delay without making Pyrrhus a desirable model: the resumed act is described as merciless slaughter. A comparison must preserve that moral discomfort.
evidence: Aroused vengeance sets him new a-work

questions.prompt: What exactly surprises Hamlet about the actor’s tears? What does his comparison leave out?
facilitatorNotes: The actor displays powerful emotion for a fictional figure with no personal connection, while Hamlet judges himself inactive despite an urgent personal cause. Tears are a performed response, however, and not the same task as deciding whether to kill; Hamlet’s self-accusation conflates those demands.
evidence: What's Hecuba to him, or he to Hecuba

questions.prompt: How does the final plan qualify Hamlet’s earlier certainty about the ghost?
facilitatorNotes: He now admits that the apparition could exploit melancholy and deceive him. The proposed performance seeks more relevant grounds in Claudius’s response. A reaction is evidence requiring interpretation, so the plan is a test rather than a guarantee of infallible knowledge.
evidence:
The spirit that I have seen
May be the devil

days.title: Hamlet — a watched encounter (III.1)
days.challenge: Interpret a celebrated speech in a scene shaped by concealment and conflicting audiences.
days.focus: The uncertainty of action and the harm caused by making another person a test.
days.context: Claudius and Polonius arrange an apparently accidental meeting between Hamlet and Ophelia. The audience sees that arrangement before Hamlet enters. The staging can leave open exactly when Hamlet suspects he is overheard; do not turn a production choice into a textual certainty.
days.contentNote: The soliloquy discusses death and suicide without prescribing either. Hamlet’s treatment of Ophelia includes sexual accusation and verbal cruelty.

excerpt.locator: Hamlet, Act/scene III.I, source blocks 1–51; opens “Scene I. A room in the castle.”; closes “King. It shall be so: Madness in great ones must not unwatch'd go. [Exeunt.”.

questions.prompt: Where does the sleep metaphor change from an argument for death into a reason to hesitate?
facilitatorNotes: Sleep initially promises an end to pain; the possibility of dreams introduces unknown experience after death. The metaphor’s own extension unsettles its apparent solution. The speech generalizes human hesitation, but its philosophical language does not remove Hamlet’s immediate distress.
evidence: To sleep: perchance to dream: ay, there's the rub

questions.prompt: What does knowing about the hidden observers change in your reading of Ophelia’s “At home”?
facilitatorNotes: The audience knows Polonius is nearby and hears an untrue answer. Ophelia is participating under family and royal authority; the line may show obedience, fear or complicity rather than freely chosen malice. The text does not explicitly identify the instant Hamlet recognizes the trap.
evidence: At home, my lord.

questions.prompt: Why do Claudius and Polonius reach different conclusions after hearing the same exchange?
facilitatorNotes: Claudius hears a dangerous hidden purpose and doubts the madness explanation; Polonius retains rejected love as the origin. Their different stakes shape interpretation. Ophelia’s lament supplies a third perspective focused on the person and relationship she believes she has lost.
evidence:
Nor what he spake, though it lack'd form a little,
Was not like madness

days.title: Hamlet — the performance as evidence (III.2 excerpt)
days.challenge: Distinguish the staged murder, onstage observers and the theatre audience’s differing knowledge.
days.focus: What a dramatic reaction can establish and what it still leaves to interpret.
days.context: Before this excerpt Hamlet coaches the actors and privately asks Horatio to watch Claudius. A silent dumb-show now precedes the spoken play. P. King and P. Queen are actors’ roles; King and Queen name Claudius and Gertrude. The excerpt ends after Hamlet and Horatio compare observations.
days.contentNote: The performance depicts poisoning, and Hamlet makes sexual taunts. The text invites scrutiny of his methods as well as Claudius’s response.

excerpt.locator: Hamlet, Act/scene III.II, source blocks 52–113; opens “Hautboys play. The dumb-show enters.”; closes “rs! For if the king like not the comedy, Why then, belike, he likes it not, perdy. Come, some music!”.

questions.prompt: Why does it matter that the audience sees the poisoning twice, first silently and then in speech and action?
facilitatorNotes: The dumb-show supplies the whole outline before the spoken performance, giving viewers time to recognize parallels. Claudius’s departure comes later, amid Hamlet’s pointed commentary. This complicates any claim that the mere sight of poison mechanically forces a unique reaction.
evidence: The Poisoner wooes the Queen with gifts

questions.prompt: How does the Player King’s account of promises challenge both the Player Queen and Hamlet?
facilitatorNotes: He argues that purpose can weaken as passions and fortunes change. The Player Queen swears permanent fidelity, while Hamlet uses her promises to test or shame his mother. The speech offers an account of change more complex than simply calling every broken promise a deliberate lie.
evidence:
What to ourselves in passion we propose,
The passion ending, doth the purpose lose.

questions.prompt: What do Hamlet and Horatio actually agree that they observed? Is Hamlet’s wager stronger than that shared observation?
facilitatorNotes: They agree Claudius reacted during the talk of poisoning; Hamlet treats that as confirmation of the ghost. The abrupt exit gives powerful support in the drama, but the men do not hear a confession here. Distinguish the observed response from the certainty Hamlet builds on it.
evidence:
I'll take the ghost's word for a
thousand pound

days.title: Hamlet — words without repentance (III.3)
days.challenge: Use dramatic irony to compare visible posture with privately spoken thought.
days.focus: The gap between guilt, attempted prayer and surrendering the gains of wrongdoing.
days.context: After the interrupted performance, Hamlet is summoned to his mother. In the omitted end of III.2 he resists his friends’ attempts to question him and prepares for that meeting. Claudius now arranges Hamlet’s departure to England, then speaks alone.
days.contentNote: The scene weighs murder, revenge and damnation within its characters’ Christian framework. It does not present Hamlet’s wish to damn another person as an uncontested moral rule.

excerpt.locator: Hamlet, Act/scene III.III, source blocks 1–16; opens “Scene III. A room in the castle.”; closes “Rising] My words fly up, my thoughts remain below: Words without thoughts never to heaven go. [Exit.”.

questions.prompt: How does Rosencrantz’s wheel image justify protecting the king, and what does it obscure?
facilitatorNotes: The image makes many lives depend on the monarch, turning royal danger into collective danger. It may describe real political consequences, but it obscures the distinction between protecting the state and protecting this ruler from accountability for his own crime.
evidence:
To whose huge spokes ten thousand lesser things
Are mortised and adjoin'd

questions.prompt: Why does Claudius believe saying “Forgive me” is insufficient?
facilitatorNotes: He retains the crown, queen and ambition for which he murdered his brother. He distinguishes corrupt earthly law, where stolen gains may purchase escape, from judgment requiring honest evidence. The speech expresses awareness and desire for relief without demonstrating completed repentance.
evidence: May one be pardon'd and retain the offence?

questions.prompt: How does the final couplet change our judgment of Hamlet’s decision to postpone killing Claudius?
facilitatorNotes: Hamlet assumes the kneeling man is being spiritually cleansed and delays in order to seek damnation as well as death. Claudius then says his thoughts remain below. The audience knows the visible prayer has failed, exposing both Hamlet’s mistaken inference and the severity of his desired revenge.
evidence: My words fly up, my thoughts remain below

days.title: Hamlet — a mirror and a hidden listener (III.4)
days.challenge: Hold incompatible accounts of perception alongside an unmistakable violent action.
days.focus: The limits of Hamlet’s claim to diagnose and reform another person.
days.context: Polonius hides behind a hanging in Gertrude’s private room. Hamlet enters after leaving Claudius at prayer. The audience is shown the hidden listener before Hamlet acts, but Gertrude does not share all of Hamlet’s knowledge.
days.contentNote: The scene includes an onstage killing, coercive family confrontation and sexually charged accusations. Gertrude’s words do not explicitly establish that she knew of the earlier murder.

excerpt.locator: Hamlet, Act/scene III.IV, source blocks 1–69; opens “Scene IV. The Queen's closet.”; closes “[Exeunt severally; Hamlet dragging in Polonius.”.

questions.prompt: How does Hamlet’s stabbing change the force of his promise to show Gertrude her inward self?
facilitatorNotes: He promises a moral mirror but almost immediately kills an unseen person without identifying him. His question about whether it is the king reveals uncertainty after the act. This rashness complicates his authority to judge her failures of perception and reason.
evidence: Nay, I know not: is it the king?

questions.prompt: What can and cannot be concluded from Gertrude’s inability to see the ghost?
facilitatorNotes: It establishes that mother and son do not share the experience in this scene. The stage direction presents a ghost to the theatre audience, while earlier watchers also saw it. A production may emphasize Hamlet’s disturbance or supernatural selectivity; the exchange alone does not erase all earlier testimony.
evidence: Nothing at all; yet all that is I see.

questions.prompt: Compare Hamlet’s account of reforming a habit with his account of killing Polonius. Where does he claim agency, and where does he shift it?
facilitatorNotes: He tells Gertrude repeated choices can change custom, giving her responsibility for action. About Polonius he expresses repentance but also casts himself as heaven’s scourge and minister. Students can find genuine moral concern while questioning whether providential language reduces his own accountability.
evidence: That I must be their scourge and minister

days.title: Hamlet — competing forms of grief (IV.4–5)
days.challenge: Compare successive scenes without assuming their characters understand one another’s circumstances.
days.focus: How martial honour and family grief are turned into calls for action.
days.context: In omitted IV.1–3, Gertrude reports Polonius’s death, Hamlet is questioned, and Claudius sends him toward England with Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, secretly requesting his execution. Hamlet now encounters Fortinbras’s army. The following scene returns to Ophelia and to Laertes, newly arrived from France.
days.contentNote: The scenes include military death, bereavement, psychological distress and a song about sexual betrayal. Ophelia’s fragmented songs should not be treated as a clinical diagnosis or a literal record of every event.

excerpt.locator: Hamlet, Act/scene IV.IV, source blocks 1–23; Act/scene IV.V, source blocks 1–78; opens “Scene IV. A plain in Denmark.”; closes “ing. So you shall; And where the offence is let the great axe fall. I pray you, go with me. [Exeunt.”.

questions.prompt: How does Hamlet’s response to the army both criticize and borrow its logic?
facilitatorNotes: He calls the disputed land a straw or eggshell and sees the terrible disproportion of lives lost for fame. Yet he uses the soldiers’ willingness to act as a rebuke to his own delay and ends by demanding bloody thoughts. The speech does not resolve the contradiction between recognizing waste and seeking a model of honour.
evidence:
That for a fantasy and trick of fame
Go to their graves like beds

questions.prompt: What warning about interpreting Ophelia does the Gentleman give before she enters? How should it affect our reading of her songs?
facilitatorNotes: Listeners piece her fragments together to fit their own thoughts. Her songs unmistakably bring grief, betrayal and sexuality into the room, but they are not a straightforward factual confession. Readers should distinguish recurring concerns from unsupported claims about exactly what happened to her.
evidence: And botch the words up fit to their own thoughts

questions.prompt: Compare Laertes’s declared willingness to risk damnation with Hamlet’s earlier concern about spiritual consequences. How does Claudius respond?
facilitatorNotes: Laertes throws conscience and both worlds aside for revenge, while Hamlet has repeatedly considered death, ghosts and salvation. Claudius redirects the immediate anger toward identifying the father’s enemies, gaining influence through apparent reasonableness. Similar grief produces different vulnerabilities.
evidence: I dare damnation

days.title: Hamlet — turning revenge into a scheme (IV.7)
days.challenge: Trace how praise, urgency and an appeal to family duty recruit a grieving person.
days.focus: The distance between professed honour and deliberately concealed violence.
days.context: In the omitted short IV.6, Horatio receives Hamlet’s letter explaining that pirates have brought him back to Denmark. Claudius has meanwhile persuaded Laertes that Hamlet killed Polonius. Another letter now announces Hamlet’s return to court.
days.contentNote: The scene plans murder and reports drowning. The circumstances and intention of Ophelia’s death remain a subject of dispute within the play.

excerpt.locator: Hamlet, Act/scene IV.VII, source blocks 1–48; opens “Scene VII. Another room in the castle.”; closes “d to do to calm his rage! Now fear I this will give it start again; Therefore let's follow. [Exeunt.”.

questions.prompt: How does Claudius move from praising Laertes’s skill to questioning his love for his father?
facilitatorNotes: Praise establishes the fencing talent needed for the scheme; the accusation of merely painted grief then pressures Laertes to demonstrate love through action. Claudius also argues that delay weakens purpose, exploiting the fear of becoming a false or inadequate son.
evidence: Or are you like the painting of a sorrow

questions.prompt: What parts of the proposed contest depend on Hamlet’s trust, and what does that reveal about the scheme’s claim to honour?
facilitatorNotes: Claudius expects Hamlet not to inspect the foils and plans to disguise the death as an accident. Laertes adds poison, and Claudius adds a second poisoned means. An apparently fair contest conceals coordinated killing; the appeal to revenge does not make its methods open or honourable.
evidence: Most generous and free from all contriving

questions.prompt: What does Gertrude’s account establish about Ophelia’s death, and what remains uncertain?
facilitatorNotes: It describes a broken branch, a fall, floating clothing, singing and eventual sinking. The picturesque natural details can convey tenderness while softening horror. It does not directly reveal Ophelia’s intention or explain Gertrude’s source of knowledge; readers should not force a definite suicide verdict from it.
evidence: As one incapable of her own distress

days.title: Hamlet — language at the grave (V.1, part 1)
days.challenge: Follow puns and changes of register as comedy approaches personal loss.
days.focus: Class, legal argument and the material equality of death.
days.context: Two grave-diggers prepare Ophelia’s grave, though Hamlet does not yet know whose funeral it is. “Clowns” names comic working characters, not costumed circus performers. Hamlet and Horatio return to encounter the first grave-digger at work.
days.contentNote: The scene discusses disputed suicide, burial exclusions and bodily decay. Its comedy and social criticism coexist with grief.

questions.prompt: How do the grave-diggers’ confused legal phrases nevertheless raise a serious question about class?
facilitatorNotes: Their parody of official reasoning is comic, but they plainly identify different treatment for a gentlewoman. The claim questions whether burial rules are applied equally. It is a criticism voiced by characters, not independent proof that Ophelia intended to die.

If this had not
been a gentlewoman

questions.prompt: How does the grave-digger’s answer about “one that was a woman” briefly overturn Hamlet’s usual verbal advantage?
facilitatorNotes: He refuses the ordinary terms of Hamlet’s questions by insisting that death changes their application. Hamlet must ask more precisely and complains about equivocation. A social inferior controls the exchange, giving practical force to the scene’s questioning of rank.
evidence: One that was a woman, sir

questions.prompt: What changes when an anonymous skull becomes Yorick’s, and why does Hamlet then turn to Alexander and Caesar?
facilitatorNotes: Imagined lawyers and courtiers permit abstract satire; recognizing someone who carried and amused him makes decay intimate and bodily. Famous conquerors then extend that personal recognition to political greatness. The imagined beer-barrel is a leveling possibility, not an archaeological claim.
evidence:
he hath borne me on his back a
thousand times

days.title: Hamlet — competing mourners and an altered letter (V.1–2 excerpts)
days.challenge: Test a protagonist’s account of responsibility against his actions and changing sympathies.
days.focus: The uneasy relation between grief, self-justification and recognition of another’s loss.
days.context: The funeral procession enters directly after the preceding night’s cemetery conversation. Hamlet discovers that Ophelia has died. The reading continues into his private account to Horatio of the voyage and the royal letter ordering his execution.
days.contentNote: The reading includes burial controversy, fighting at a grave and the forging of an execution order. Hamlet’s self-defence remains open to ethical evaluation.

questions.prompt: What happens to Ophelia’s funeral when Hamlet and Laertes compete over the extent of their grief?
facilitatorNotes: The woman being buried becomes the occasion for a contest of love, self-display and physical aggression. Both can feel genuine grief, yet extravagant numbers and impossible acts shift attention toward the men. Gertrude’s wedding flowers and the priest’s limited rites offer different ways of framing the loss.
evidence:
forty thousand brothers
Could not, with all their quantity of love,
Make up my sum

questions.prompt: How does Hamlet defend sending Rosencrantz and Guildenstern to death? What would be needed to evaluate his defence fully?
facilitatorNotes: He says they eagerly accepted their employment and placed themselves between powerful opponents. The intercepted execution order proves a threat to him; it does not by itself establish how much the bearers knew. His lack of remorse and class language therefore require scrutiny rather than automatic endorsement.
evidence: They are not near my conscience

questions.prompt: Why does Hamlet’s recognition of Laertes’s “cause” matter after the graveyard quarrel? Does it undo the harm?
facilitatorNotes: He recognizes another son’s grief through the image of his own, a capacity absent from the competitive outburst. He admits losing control and proposes reconciliation. The recognition changes his account but cannot restore Polonius or Ophelia or ensure Laertes will abandon revenge.

For, by the image of my cause, I see
The portraiture of his

days.title: Hamlet — readiness, forgiveness and the surviving story (V.2 conclusion)
days.challenge: Integrate visible action, delayed testimony and competing interpretations of a tragic ending.
days.focus: Who survives to tell the story, and how a political conclusion shapes a personal one.
days.context: In the omitted middle of V.2, the courtier Osric proposes the fencing wager and Hamlet accepts. The audience knows about the poisoned blade and cup; Hamlet does not. Horatio now voices concern. This selection supplies the play’s conclusion, following the evidence and judgments developed across the preceding nights.
days.contentNote: The conclusion includes multiple deaths by poisoned weapons and drink, and Horatio briefly proposes dying with Hamlet. Hamlet instead insists that his friend live to testify.

questions.prompt: How can “the readiness is all” sound both different from Hamlet’s earlier deliberations and troubling in this situation?
facilitatorNotes: He accepts uncertainty and mortality instead of trying to control every consequence; that can suggest composure. Yet he refuses a friend’s practical offer to postpone a dangerous encounter. The audience’s knowledge of the trap permits a reading that sees acceptance and imprudence together.
evidence: the readiness is all

questions.prompt: How does the language of responsibility change between Hamlet’s initial apology and Laertes’s final confession?
facilitatorNotes: Hamlet acknowledges wrong but separates his self from the madness that supposedly acted. Laertes finally identifies the treachery, admits its return upon himself and names Claudius. Their exchange of forgiveness occurs after concealed causes become public, though forgiveness does not erase the deaths.
evidence: I am justly kill'd with mine own treachery

questions.prompt: Why is Horatio required to live, and how does Fortinbras’s final tribute complicate the story he must tell?
facilitatorNotes: Hamlet fears a wounded name if the causes remain unknown and asks his friend to testify. Fortinbras immediately supplies a soldierly, royal frame for someone whose course has been far less simple. The ending combines the need for an accurate narrative with a new ruler’s interest in a usable public ceremony.
evidence: Bear Hamlet, like a soldier, to the stage
